summary: This tutorial presents a comprehensive experimental workflow for characterizing and calibrating tunable transmon qubits, demonstrated on a commercial five-qubit Soprano-D2 processor in a dilution refrigerator. The paper details procedures from cryogenic setup through parametric amplifier optimization, flux sweet-spot identification, pulse calibration, readout optimization, and qubit-qubit coupling characterization, with emphasis on practical considerations and expected parameter ranges.
motivation: While the theoretical principles of transmon control are well established, experimentalists face significant practical challenges in bringing up superconducting quantum devices, requiring repeated discovery of procedures, calibration heuristics, and failure modes that vary with specific hardware and wiring schemes.
method: The authors applied a systematic sequence of spectroscopy and calibration measurements to a five-qubit coupled transmon chip, including VNA-based resonator spectroscopy, one-tone and two-tone qubit spectroscopy, Rabi oscillations for pulse calibration, dispersive readout optimization via $IQ$ diagrams, avoided-level-crossing measurements for coupling characterization, and deterministic benchmarking for error quantification.
result: Representative results show: flux sweet-spot identification via $\omega_q(\Phi)$ mapping; Rabi calibration of $\pi$ and $\pi/2$ pulses with linewidth control (15–43 MHz depending on drive power $-66$ to $-72$ dBm); anharmonicity $\alpha \approx 200$–300 MHz from two-tone and one-photon spectroscopy; readout fidelities up to $\sim 0.95$ with optimized pulse durations ($\geq 1500$ ns); qubit–qubit coupling strength $J \approx 3.0$ MHz from avoided crossing; and error characterization yielding $T_1 \approx 24.5$ µs, $T_2 \approx 9.3$ µs, rotation errors $\delta\theta \approx 2.2°$, and phase errors $\delta\phi \approx 1.0°$.
